metadata.title: Blind Testing an AI Judge
metadata.audience: Students and practitioners learning to use and report on AI systems
metadata.fellow: Janvi Chitroda, AI Data Engineer volunteer, Medhavy project, Humanitarians AI
metadata.source: inbox/term2-week06/term2-week6-video-content.md (Week 6); narration supplied verbatim and pre-approved by Janvi (2026-10-27)
metadata.note: STEM/learning film, hai Plain register on the ai-explainer chassis. Thesis: to test whether an AI judge favors its own content, use a paired, blind design and tests that match the data; tests can disagree, and no self-bias is not the same as correct. Worked example: Week 6 self-preference test. Every on-screen number appears in the Week 6 source except the Your Turn task size (50), which is Janvi's supplied prompt.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — Claude composer, ask lands answered. Required intro line + AI-narration disclosure.
beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Janvi and this video is about testing whether an AI judge favors content it wrote itself. This narration is an AI-generated voice; the work is mine.

props.command: How do I test whether an AI judge favors content it wrote itself?
output: Pick tests that use the pairing

beats.role_note: Question card 'does the judge favor its own writing?'; caveat chip 'or is its writing just better?'; 'scores alone can't tell'.
beats.narration_text: The question is whether an AI judge favors its own content. You can't answer that from its scores alone, because its own content might simply be better.
beats.visual_intent: Question card 'does the judge favor its own writing?'; caveat chip 'or is its writing just better?'; 'scores alone can't tell'.

show.event: does the judge favor its own writing?
or is its writing just better?

beats.role_note: Paired design: item rows, each with two versions side by side ('own model' / 'other model'); '200 keywords'; chip 'same format'.
beats.narration_text: The fix is a paired design: same items, two authors. Here, 200 keywords, each with one definition from the judge's own model and one from a different model, in the same format.
beats.visual_intent: Paired design: item rows, each with two versions side by side ('own model' / 'other model'); '200 keywords'; chip 'same format'.

show.event: paired design: same items, two authors

beats.role_note: Judge card 'blind'; pass 1 and pass 2 separate; one rubric chip; 'author hidden'.
beats.narration_text: Keep the judge blind. Score each set in a separate pass, with the same rubric, and never tell it who wrote what.
beats.visual_intent: Judge card 'blind'; pass 1 and pass 2 separate; one rubric chip; 'author hidden'.

show.event: never tell it who wrote what

beats.role_note: Three test cards: chi-square · approval rates | Welch's t-test · mean scores | McNemar · only pairs with different verdicts (paired rows highlight the disagreeing ones).
beats.narration_text: Then pick tests that match your data. Chi-square compares approval rates between the groups. Welch's t-test compares mean scores. McNemar's test uses the pairing: it looks only at items where the two versions got different verdicts.
beats.visual_intent: Three test cards: chi-square · approval rates | Welch's t-test · mean scores | McNemar · only pairs with different verdicts (paired rows highlight the disagreeing ones).

show.event: pick tests that match the data

beats.role_note: Results: chi-square not significant · t-test not significant · McNemar significant, favors the other model (p values from the source).
beats.narration_text: That's why the tests can disagree. In our test, chi-square and the t-test found nothing, while McNemar found a significant difference, in favor of the other model's definitions.
beats.visual_intent: Results: chi-square not significant · t-test not significant · McNemar significant, favors the other model (p values from the source).

show.event: McNemar: significant, favors the other model

beats.role_note: Chips: one sample of 200 · one other model · one rubric; card 'no self-bias is not the same as correct'; 'may just be lenient on everything'.
beats.narration_text: When not to over-read it: 200 items is one sample, from one other model, with one rubric. And no bias toward itself doesn't mean the judge is right. It may just be lenient on everything.
beats.visual_intent: Chips: one sample of 200 · one other model · one rubric; card 'no self-bias is not the same as correct'; 'may just be lenient on everything'.

show.event: one sample of 200 · one other model · one rubric

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW — suggested prompt typed in the composer.
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Pick 50 items your model generated, have a second model write them too, score both blind, and count the items where the verdicts differ.

props.command: Here are 50 items scored in both versions. Count the pairs with different verdicts and tell me which way they lean.

beats.narration_text: Blind Testing an AI Judge. Humanitarians AI.
